name: The Cartography Hearings — Live Public Tribunal, 2213
creator: Meridian Civil Accountability Forum (independent civic body)
description: From March through June 2213, the Meridian Civil Accountability Forum conducted open public hearings into corporate infrastructure liability following the Lakefire Collapse of 2211, broadcasting every session live on both licensed and pirate neural feeds simultaneously — a deliberate choice to prevent any single corponation from controlling access. Over 14 weeks and 62 sessions, testimony from survivors, engineers, corporate representatives, and Municipal Safety officials was heard; the hearings drew larger sustained neural audiences than any sporting event in Meridian history. The final session, in which a HelixCorp logistics director broke from prepared testimony and spoke without corporate counsel present, was watched by an estimated 11 million people.
medium: live neural feed, pirate broadcast simultaneous, physical gallery seating
cultural_impact: The Cartography Hearings established the template for civilian-led accountability processes in GLMZ and produced the Infrastructure Liability Compact of 2214, the first legally binding constraint on corporate sovereignty in public space in forty years.
controversy: HelixCorp and Axiom both attempted injunctions against the simultaneous pirate broadcast on grounds of signal sovereignty; both were denied by the Tribunal on the novel argument that civic testimony is inherently public domain. The legal precedent has been contested ever since.
story_hooks: The HelixCorp logistics director who broke from prepared testimony vanished from their registered address two days after the final session; their corporate access credentials were used once more, six months later, in a facility in Tier 1.

Session 34 of the hearings was broadcast with a 90-second gap — officially attributed to technical failure — during which, according to gallery witnesses, a document was briefly displayed and then removed from the record.
A character is approached by someone claiming to have the unredacted engineering reports submitted to the Tribunal — reports that differ significantly from the public record.
